## navigation

### NAV-001 — Work areas first, account last

**Rule:** Fill the main menu with the core objects or jobs of the product, ordered by how often they are used in daily work, and place account and admin entries last, visually separated.

- Why: Users open the dashboard to do recurring work; putting the daily queue at the top and rare administration at the bottom shortens the most common path and keeps configuration out of the way.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any dashboard with a persistent left sidebar.
- Exceptions: Products organised as a catalogue of independent services may order groups by product family instead of frequency, but still keep account administration last.
- Do: Home, Orders, Products, Customers, Reports ... then a separator, then Settings at the bottom.
- Don't: Billing, Users and API keys mixed between Orders and Products in the main list.
- Check (static): In the nav config or screenshot, list top-level items in order; verify the first item is the landing page or the main work queue, that no settings, billing, members, API or account entry appears above the last core work item, and that those entries sit after a separator or in a bottom block.
- Check (live): Open the dashboard at 1440 px; read the sidebar top to bottom in the accessibility tree; confirm account/settings entries are the last group and separated (separator element, gap or footer region).

### NAV-002 — Noun labels in sentence case

**Rule:** Label every menu item with a short noun or noun phrase for the object or task area, in sentence case, never with a verb.

- Why: Menu items name places to go, while verbs belong to buttons; noun labels stay stable as features grow and match the page title users land on.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: All sidebar items, group labels and sub-items.
- Exceptions: Proper product names keep their own capitalisation.
- Do: Orders, Pickups, Traffic policies, Address book.
- Don't: Create shipment, Manage Users, VIEW REPORTS.
- Check (static): Grep the nav definition for labels; flag any label starting with a verb (create, add, manage, view, edit, go) or written in Title Case or ALL CAPS; verify each label matches the H1 of its target page.
- Check (live): Read every sidebar link name in the accessibility tree and confirm none starts with a verb and none is in Title Case or ALL CAPS (proper names excepted); then click each top-level item and confirm the page H1 uses the same words, singular/plural included.

### NAV-003 — Icons and collapsible icon rail

**Rule:** Give each top-level item an icon and let users collapse the sidebar to an icon rail that keeps the same icons, with the label available as a tooltip and accessible name.

- Why: A collapsed rail returns width to dense pages without hiding navigation, and stable icons let users find items in both states.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Desktop and tablet widths with a persistent sidebar.
- Exceptions: Small utility links in a bottom block (logs, support) may be text-only while expanded, but they still need an icon if they stay visible in the rail.
- Do: Toggle button labelled "Collapse navigation" / "Expand navigation"; rail shows the same icons; hover shows the label.
- Don't: Collapsed rail with unlabeled icons that have no tooltip or aria-label, or a rail that drops items.
- Check (static): Verify every top-level nav item has an icon prop; verify a collapse toggle exists with an aria-label and aria-expanded; verify rail items keep the label as aria-label or visually hidden text.
- Check (live): Click the collapse toggle at 1440 px; confirm all top-level items remain as icons, each has an accessible name in the accessibility tree, a tooltip with the label appears on hover and on keyboard focus, and the toggle's aria-expanded flips.

### NAV-004 — Clear active state

**Rule:** Mark the current destination with a filled highlight on the item itself, set aria-current="page" on it, and keep its parent expanded when the active page is a sub-item.

- Why: Users must always know where they are; a highlighted item plus an expanded parent replaces the need for a breadcrumb on top-level pages.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Every page reachable from the sidebar, including detail pages of an object (highlight the object's list item).
- Exceptions: None.
- Do: Orders > Drafts open: Orders expanded, Drafts highlighted, Drafts has aria-current=page.
- Don't: Highlight shown only by a colour change of the icon, or no item highlighted on a detail page.
- Check (static): Verify the nav component sets an active class and aria-current="page" based on the current route, including route prefixes for detail pages; verify the active style differs by more than colour alone (background fill or weight).
- Check (live): Open a list page, a detail page and a sub-item page; in the accessibility tree confirm exactly one link has aria-current=page (or is the selected item), and its parent shows expanded.

### NAV-005 — Group and nest only when the menu is large

**Rule:** Keep the menu as a flat list when it has about ten or fewer destinations; above that, add labeled groups, and show sub-items only under their parent through a disclosure.

- Why: Small tools work faster with one flat list, while large multi-product consoles need labeled groups and nesting to stay scannable.
- Confidence: low (source inferred; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Deciding the menu structure; the threshold is inferred from a flat 9-item menu versus a large labeled product menu.
- Exceptions: Products with dozens of services may nest deeper than one level; then give every group a label and keep a search over all pages. Installable extensions get their own group regardless of size (see NAV-010).
- Do: 9 jobs as one flat list; a 40-destination console split into labeled groups like Build and Protect, each with collapsible items.
- Don't: Three-level nesting in a menu with 8 destinations, or 30 ungrouped items in one list.
- Check (static): Count top-level destinations in the nav config; if more than about 10, verify group labels exist; verify sub-items render only inside a disclosure under their parent and that depth beyond 2 levels has a written justification.
- Check (live): Expand every group; record max depth and items per group; confirm sub-items are hidden until the parent is opened or active, and disclosure buttons expose aria-expanded.

### NAV-006 — Drawer on narrow screens

**Rule:** Below tablet width, hide the sidebar behind a single menu control that opens a drawer, instead of keeping a sidebar that squeezes the content.

- Why: On phones every pixel of width goes to the task; a persistent rail or expanded menu pushes tables and forms into horizontal scroll.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Viewports below about 768 px; between 768 px and 1024 px an icon rail is acceptable.
- Exceptions: None for the main nav; secondary navs (settings, product sub-nav) follow the same rule.
- Do: At 390 px: a labelled "Menu" button opens a drawer with focus trapped and a close control; content uses the full width.
- Don't: At 390 px an icon rail plus an expanded settings sidebar leave the form a third of the screen.
- Check (static): Verify CSS/layout breakpoints switch the sidebar to a drawer below the mobile breakpoint, with a toggle that has aria-expanded and aria-controls, and that the drawer traps focus and closes on Escape.
- Check (live): Load home and a settings page at 390 px and 768 px; confirm no sidebar is visible at 390 px, the menu button opens a drawer, Escape closes it, focus returns to the button, and the page has no horizontal scroll.

### NAV-009 — Sidebar swaps for child scope

**Rule:** When the user enters a child scope (one site, project or zone inside an account), replace the sidebar with that scope's menu, headed by a back link to the parent list.

- Why: Child scopes have their own feature set; swapping the menu keeps it short and tells users which level they are configuring.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify absent, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Products with nested scopes where each child has many feature pages.
- Exceptions: When a child scope only changes values (for example a market or region overriding defaults), handle it inside the page with inherited versus customised states, not by swapping the sidebar.
- Do: Inside one zone: sidebar headed "Back to Domains" plus the zone name, then the zone's own groups.
- Don't: Account-level and zone-level items mixed in one menu with no indication of the level.
- Check (static): Verify child-scope routes render a separate nav config whose first item is a back link to the parent list and whose header names the child scope.
- Check (live): Open a child scope from its list; confirm the sidebar changes, shows the child name and a back link, and the back link returns to the parent list with the original sidebar.

### NAV-010 — Separate slot for extensions

**Rule:** Put items added by installed apps or extensions in a labeled, collapsible group below the core items, and let users pin, reorder or unpin them.

- Why: Extensions vary per customer; a dedicated slot keeps the core menu stable and stops third-party items from pushing core work down.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Products where third parties or users can install apps, channels or plugins that have their own pages.
- Exceptions: Integrations that only sync data and have no pages add no menu items; they live in settings.
- Do: "Apps >" group under core items; an open app shows its own sub-items (including its Settings) under its entry, and an app's own sub-menu shows at most 6 items before "View more".
- Don't: Each installed app appended to the core list, or extension pages reachable only through settings.
- Check (static): Verify extension nav items come from a separate registry rendered in its own labeled, collapsible group after the core items, with pin/unpin actions, and that an open extension's sub-items render only under its own entry.
- Check (live): Install or enable an extension in a test account; confirm it appears only in the extension group, can be pinned and unpinned, and core item order is unchanged.

### NAV-011 — Counts only for work queues

**Rule:** Use numeric badges only for actionable queues (items waiting for the user), use text pills for lifecycle labels such as New or Beta, and keep counts visible at every width.

- Why: A number in the menu is a call to act; showing it for non-actionable totals trains users to ignore it, and losing it on small screens hides pending work.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any item with a queue of work (unfulfilled orders, items to print, reviews to approve).
- Exceptions: Queue products may show per-state counters as tabs on the list page instead of a menu badge; then the same counts must survive narrow layouts.
- Do: Orders badge "3" = 3 orders to fulfil, with accessible name "Orders, 3 to fulfil"; feature pill "Beta".
- Don't: Badge with total customers; counters that disappear below 768 px with no replacement.
- Check (static): List every badge source; verify numeric badges map to an actionable query, have an accessible text including what is counted, and are not hidden by a responsive CSS rule.
- Check (live): Create one pending item in a test account; confirm the badge increments, its accessible name says what is counted, and it is still visible (or in the drawer) at 768 px and 390 px.

### NAV-012 — Personalise without breaking the core

**Rule:** Let users pin, hide or reach recent items in the menu, keep core items fixed in place, and store the choice per user, not per browser.

- Why: Different roles use different parts of a product; personalisation trims noise, while fixed core positions keep shared instructions and muscle memory valid. Per-user storage is inferred, because the one observed hide preference was saved per browser only.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Menus with more items than a single role uses daily, or with installable extensions.
- Exceptions: Home and Settings can never be hidden.
- Do: Pin a page to a Pinned/Recents block; hide unused items from a preference page; preference follows the user to another device.
- Don't: Hide preference saved only in this browser, or drag-reordering that moves Home and Settings.
- Check (static): Verify pin/hide/recents state is persisted through a user preference API, not localStorage alone; verify Home and Settings are excluded from hide/reorder.
- Check (live): Pin and hide an item, log out, log in from a fresh browser profile; confirm the same menu appears and that Home and Settings cannot be hidden.

## settings

### SET-001 — Work in the menu, rare configuration in settings

**Rule:** Put the objects and jobs people touch every day in the main menu, and put rarely changed account-wide configuration behind a settings or account-admin entry that is separate from those work items.

- Why: Frequency decides placement: the menu is scanned many times a day, so every item that is used once a quarter costs attention on every visit.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any admin dashboard with both day-to-day work objects (orders, products, records) and account configuration (defaults, connections, billing).
- Exceptions: An urgent, instant on/off control that people reach for during an incident (for example an emergency protection mode or a maintenance mode) may sit on the object's overview page, with its full configuration still in settings.
- Do: Menu: Home, Orders, Products, Customers, Reports. Settings: Payments, Taxes, Shipping defaults, Users, Billing.
- Don't: A top-level menu item 'Tax rates' or 'Label format' next to 'Orders'.
- Check (static): List every top-level work item in the main menu (excluding the separated settings or account-admin group) and every settings page. Flag any work item whose page is mostly form controls for account-wide defaults, and any settings page that holds a queue or list of daily work records.
- Check (live): Open the main menu and click each top-level work item; each must land on a list, queue or overview of work, not on a configuration form. Open settings and confirm no page there is a daily work queue.

### SET-002 — Per-object configuration on the object

**Rule:** Put configuration that belongs to one object on that object's own page, as a section or a Settings tab, never in global settings.

- Why: People change an object's options while looking at the object; sending them to global settings breaks the task and hides which object the option belongs to.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: A setting changes the behaviour or data of one record (one product, one shipment, one service, one integration).
- Exceptions: A default that applies to all new objects belongs in settings; the object page then shows the per-object value and may override it (see SET-011). Objects that are themselves configuration (integrations, connections, notification templates) may have their list and detail pages inside settings; their options still sit on each object's own detail page.
- Do: Product page with a status, package and custom fields section; a service detail page with tabs Overview, Metrics, Settings.
- Don't: Settings > Products > choose a product from a dropdown > edit its options.
- Check (static): For each settings page, check whether any field needs an object picker (a select or search listing individual records) before it can be edited. Each such field must move to that object's detail page.
- Check (live): Open one object's detail page and confirm its own options are editable there (inline section or Settings tab). Open every shared settings page (one not dedicated to a single object) and confirm none has a field that edits only this object.

### SET-003 — Sub-area settings inside the sub-area

**Rule:** When the product has distinct sub-products, channels or installed apps, give each its own Settings item inside its own navigation group, at the same position in every group, preferably last.

- Why: Settings that only make sense inside one sub-area are found faster next to what they control, and the global settings list stays short.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The dashboard hosts several sub-products, channels or third-party apps, each with its own navigation group and its own settings.
- Exceptions: A single-product tool with one coherent job (for example a shipping tool with about 25 settings pages) may keep all settings in one central area grouped by lifecycle; one of the reference portals does this successfully. The global settings may still list installed apps and channels, linking into each one's own Settings.
- Do: Sidebar group 'Email' with items Campaigns, Templates, Email settings; global settings only lists 'Apps and channels'.
- Don't: Global settings with 40 entries, half of them named after individual apps or sub-products.
- Check (static): For each sub-product or app navigation group, check that it contains one item labelled 'Settings' or '<Name> settings', at the same position in every group. Check that global settings holds no page specific to only one sub-product.
- Check (live): Open each sub-product group in the sidebar and confirm it has a settings item in the same position as in the other groups, and that it opens a page scoped to that sub-product. Open global settings and confirm it contains no sub-product-only options.

### SET-004 — Settings as a mode with its own navigation

**Rule:** When the user enters settings, show a dedicated settings navigation that replaces or sits beside the main menu, with a labelled link back to the main menu, and give every settings page its own URL.

- Why: A dedicated list keeps all settings pages one click apart and tells the user they are configuring, not working; the back link and real URLs prevent dead ends and allow sharing and bookmarking a page.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Settings span more than one page.
- Exceptions: A short settings area of one page with tabs needs no separate navigation, but each tab should still change the URL; one reference portal has no settings mode and uses tabs without URL changes for account configuration, which blocks deep links.
- Do: Entering settings collapses the main menu to an icon rail and opens a second column headed 'Back to main menu' listing every settings page; each item is a link to /settings/<page>.
- Don't: Settings pages reachable only by a chain of cards from an overview, with no persistent list and no way back other than the browser button.
- Check (static): Check the settings layout renders a navigation list of all settings pages plus a back control whose text or accessible name says where it goes. Check each list item is an anchor with a distinct route.
- Check (live): Open settings; confirm the settings list is visible and the back link returns to the main menu. Click three settings pages and confirm the URL changes each time; reload each URL and confirm the same page opens.

### SET-005 — Fixed settings entry at the sidebar bottom

**Rule:** Place the settings entry at the bottom of the main sidebar, separated from the work items, in the same spot on every page.

- Why: A fixed, predictable spot lets people return to rarely used configuration without searching, and the separation signals it is not daily work.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The dashboard has a persistent left sidebar.
- Exceptions: Personal account details (own email, password) may also be reachable from the profile menu (see SET-008). With no sidebar, use the profile or account menu as the single entry.
- Do: Sidebar bottom block: Settings (gear icon), then account and profile.
- Don't: Settings as the fourth item between Orders and Products, or reachable only from a link on the home page.
- Check (static): Check the sidebar component places the settings link after all work items, in a separate group or below a divider, and that it is rendered on every route.
- Check (live): On home, a list page and a detail page, confirm the settings entry is at the bottom of the sidebar in the same position. At narrow width, confirm it is still reachable from the collapsed menu or drawer.

### SET-006 — Settings entry opens the first settings page

**Rule:** Make the settings entry land directly on the first, most used settings page with the full settings list visible, instead of on a separate overview of cards.

- Why: An overview page adds a click to every visit; with the list always visible, the user can jump to any page from the first screen.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Settings have an internal navigation list (SET-004).
- Exceptions: When settings span several scopes (personal, account, sub-product), an entry page that routes to each scope can be acceptable, as long as each scope then follows this rule.
- Do: Clicking Settings opens /settings/general, with the list of all settings pages on the left.
- Don't: Clicking Settings opens a grid of 20 tiles that each must be clicked to see any setting.
- Check (static): Check that the /settings route redirects or renders the first settings page, and that the first item in the settings navigation matches it.
- Check (live): Click the settings entry; confirm the first screen shows real settings controls or values plus the settings navigation, with the first navigation item marked active.

### SET-007 — One grouping axis per settings level

**Rule:** Group the settings list by one stable mental model per level (business domain, workflow phase, or product) and add short group headings once the list passes about 20 entries.

- Why: A single axis lets the user predict where a setting lives; mixing axes at one level makes the same setting plausible in two places.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Designing the settings navigation or splitting a long settings page into sections.
- Exceptions: The portals agree on one axis per level but not on which axis; choose the one that matches the user's job (workflow phase for operational tools, business domain for commerce, product for multi-product platforms). The 20-entry threshold is inferred: one portal lists 19 entries flat, another groups 24 entries under 6 headings.
- Do: Groups General, Connect, Order management, Shipping, After purchase, Account, each with 3 to 5 pages.
- Don't: One flat list mixing 'Payments', 'Step 3: shipping', 'Advanced' and 'Webhooks' at the same level.
- Check (static): Write each settings group and page name in a table with its grouping axis (domain, phase, product). Flag any level whose names use more than one axis, and any list over 20 entries with no group headings.
- Check (live): Open settings and read the navigation; confirm headings exist when there are more than 20 entries. Pick three settings (for example the default currency, the timezone, the API key) and confirm each is listed under exactly one group heading.

### SET-008 — Personal preferences apart from account settings

**Rule:** Put a person's own preferences and credentials (language, theme, timezone, shortcuts, own email and password, personal tokens) on a personal profile page, separate from settings that affect the whole account.

- Why: Account settings change things for everyone and may need admin rights; personal preferences change only the viewer. Mixing them hides who is affected by a change.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The dashboard has more than one user per account, or has per-user preferences such as theme or shortcuts.
- Exceptions: A single-user tool may keep personal items in settings, but should still group them on one page labelled as personal; one reference portal mixes dark mode and menu visibility into account settings.
- Do: Profile menu > Profile: Language, Appearance, Timezone, Keyboard shortcuts, Password. Settings > General: Business name, Currency.
- Don't: Settings > Interface page with dark mode next to account-wide label format and currency.
- Check (static): Tag each settings field as 'affects only me' or 'affects the account'. Every 'only me' field must live under the profile route; every 'account' field under settings.
- Check (live): Open the profile or user menu and confirm it leads to the personal page with language, theme and timezone. Open each account settings page and confirm none of those personal controls appears there. With two users, change the theme as user A and confirm user B does not see the change.

### SET-009 — Account administration lives in settings

**Rule:** Put plan and billing, users and roles, API keys and tokens, and the audit log behind the settings or account-admin entry, never as work items in the main menu.

- Why: These pages are visited rarely, by admins, and carry risk; keeping them together behind one entry makes them easy to find and easy to restrict by role.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The product has billing, multiple users, programmatic access or an audit trail.
- Exceptions: A product whose billing happens outside the dashboard may omit a billing page. The audit log placement varies across the reference portals (inside settings, in an account-admin group, or a top-level Logs area); any of these is acceptable if it sits outside the main work items, in the separated bottom block of the sidebar or in the account menu.
- Do: Settings (or a separated 'Manage account' group at the sidebar bottom): Plan, Billing, Users, API tokens, Audit log.
- Don't: Main menu items 'Billing' and 'API keys' between 'Orders' and 'Reports'.
- Check (static): Check that billing, users, API key and audit log routes are under the settings or account-admin route prefix (or, for the audit log, a logs route linked from the sidebar bottom block) and are absent from the main work menu.
- Check (live): Open the main menu and confirm none of billing, users, API keys, audit log is a work item. From the settings or account-admin entry, reach each of them within two clicks.

### SET-010 — Current value visible without opening an editor

**Rule:** Show the current value or state of every setting on its settings page, either as the live control or as a summary row with the value, so the user can scan before editing.

- Why: People return to settings mostly to check what is set; hiding values behind 'Edit' buttons forces a click per setting just to read it.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Every settings page.
- Exceptions: Secrets (API keys, passwords) show a masked value or 'Set' state rather than the value itself.
- Do: Row 'Local delivery - Off >' or a switch that reads On; a select showing 'EUR'.
- Don't: A row that reads only 'Shipping rates' with an 'Edit' button and no hint of what is configured.
- Check (static): For each setting row in the spec or screenshot, check that a current value, state word, count or live control is visible next to its label.
- Check (live): Open each settings page without clicking anything; confirm every setting shows its current value or state. Change one setting, return to the page, and confirm the new value is shown.

### SET-011 — Inherited defaults with visible overrides

**Rule:** When an object or sub-account can override an account default, show on that object whether each value is inherited or customised, and where the default comes from.

- Why: Without the inherited/customised marker the user cannot tell whether changing the global default will affect this object, or why two objects behave differently.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: A setting exists both as an account default and as a per-object or per-sub-account value (for example a regional market, a child account, a location).
- Exceptions: When an object has no override capability, show only its effective value.
- Do: Market page with two groups, 'Customized' and 'Inherited', each inherited item labelled 'Inherited from store default'.
- Don't: A per-object currency field prefilled with the default, with no way to tell whether it is a copy or a live link.
- Check (static): For each setting that has both a default and a per-object value, check the object view marks it as inherited or customised and names the source of the inherited value.
- Check (live): Change the account default; open an object that inherits it and confirm the new value appears marked as inherited. Override it on the object and confirm the marker switches to customised.

### SET-012 — Search across settings

**Rule:** Offer a search that finds settings by name, inside the settings area or in a global quick search that indexes settings pages.

- Why: Users remember the name of a setting more often than which group it lives in, especially when the list is long or grouped by an axis they do not share.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Settings span more than about 15 pages or are spread across several scopes.
- Exceptions: A settings area of a few pages, all visible in one list, does not need its own search.
- Do: A 'Search settings' field at the top of the settings navigation; typing 'currency' lists General > Store defaults.
- Don't: Global search that only finds records (orders, customers) and never settings pages.
- Check (static): Check that a settings search field exists in the settings navigation or that the global search index includes settings pages and section titles.
- Check (live): Type the name of a setting that lives two levels deep (for example 'timezone') into the search; confirm a result names that setting and opens the settings page that holds it.

## global-chrome

### CHR-001 — Global search always in the chrome

**Rule:** Put one global search entry in the persistent chrome so it is visible and reachable from every page, in the same place on every page.

- Why: Search is the escape hatch when the menu does not match the user's mental model; if it lives only on some pages, users must first navigate to find the thing that helps them navigate.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any dashboard with more than a handful of pages or with searchable objects (orders, products, records).
- Exceptions: Placement varies (top of the sidebar or the top bar); pick one and keep it fixed. A product whose only searchable object is one record type may scope the global search to that type, but it must say so in the placeholder.
- Do: A "Search" button at the top of the sidebar on every page, including settings and detail pages.
- Don't: Search only as a field on the home page, or only as a menu item that leads to a separate search page.
- Check (static): In the layout/shell component, verify the search trigger is rendered by the shared chrome (not by individual pages); verify every route uses that shell, including settings and scoped sub-areas.
- Check (live): Visit home, an index, a detail and a settings page at 1440 px; on each, find a control named "Search" (or a combobox/searchbox) in the banner or sidebar landmark, at the same position.

### CHR-002 — Cmd/Ctrl+K opens search everywhere

**Rule:** Open global search with Cmd+K on macOS and Ctrl+K elsewhere from any page, show the hint next to the trigger, and also accept "/" when focus is not in a text field.

- Why: A single well-known hotkey turns search into the fastest route to any page or record, and showing the hint on the trigger teaches it without documentation.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Desktop web dashboards with a global search or command palette.
- Exceptions: Do not capture "/" or the hotkey while the user is typing in an input, textarea or contenteditable; on touch-only layouts the hint is hidden.
- Do: Trigger reads "Search... ⌘K"; pressing Cmd+K on a settings page opens the same dialog with the input focused.
- Don't: A search icon with no hotkey, or a hotkey that only works on the home page.
- Check (static): Grep for a global keydown handler registered in the app shell for meta/ctrl+k and "/"; verify it ignores events whose target is an editable element; verify the trigger renders a kbd hint.
- Check (live): On three different pages press Cmd/Ctrl+K; a dialog opens with focus in a combobox/searchbox; press Escape and focus returns to the previously focused element; type "/" inside a form field and confirm it types a slash and does not open search.

### CHR-003 — Search dialog that guides before typing

**Rule:** Show recent items and search scopes or filters as soon as the search dialog opens, group results by type with a breadcrumb or parent label, and show keyboard hints in the dialog footer.

- Why: An empty input gives no clue about what can be found; recents cover the most common repeat visits, scopes narrow large result sets, and parent labels disambiguate items with the same name.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any global search or command palette that searches pages, settings and records together.
- Exceptions: A search limited to one object type can skip scope chips but still shows recents.
- Do: On open: "Recents" group (5 items, each with its area name), a row of scope chips (Orders, Products, Customers, Settings), footer "↑ ↓ to navigate, ↵ to select, Esc to close".
- Don't: A blank input with no suggestions, and a flat result list where two "Settings" entries cannot be told apart.
- Check (static): In the search component, verify an initial state that renders recents (and scopes/filters) without a query, result items with a group and a parent/breadcrumb label, loading and empty states, and a footer with key hints.
- Check (live): Open search without typing; confirm a listbox with at least a "Recents" group is present; type a term that matches pages in two areas and confirm results are grouped and each shows its parent; type nonsense and confirm an explicit "no results" message; use arrow keys and Enter to open a result.

### CHR-004 — Discoverable keyboard shortcut map

**Rule:** When the product has keyboard shortcuts, open a dialog listing all of them on "?", and use two-key sequences with a consistent first letter per intent (g for go to, a or c for add or create).

- Why: Shortcuts nobody can find are dead weight; a "?" sheet is the convention power users try first, and consistent prefixes make shortcuts guessable.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Dashboards used daily by the same people, with recurring navigation or creation tasks.
- Exceptions: Task-specific keys (Enter to print in a scan workflow, Space and arrows for drag and drop) may live only in their own screen, but they still appear in the "?" sheet under that screen's group.
- Do: "?" opens "Keyboard shortcuts": Go to (g h Home, g o Orders, g s Settings), Create (a p Add product), Page (s focus Save bar, f focus filters).
- Don't: Undocumented single letters scattered per page, or the same first letter meaning "settings" in one place and "switch" in another.
- Check (static): Verify a single shortcut registry (one file or table) that both the key handler and the "?" dialog read from; check that every sequence's first key maps to one intent only.
- Check (live): Press "?" outside a text field; a dialog lists shortcuts grouped by intent; try two listed sequences (one navigation, one action) and confirm each does what the sheet says; press Escape to close.

### CHR-005 — Shortcuts and search follow renames

**Rule:** Generate shortcut labels, shortcut targets and the search index from the same navigation config, and keep the old name as a search alias after a rename.

- Why: Hand-maintained shortcut maps drift; after an area is renamed or a page removed, shortcuts keep the old name or lead to a redirect or a not-found page, which erodes trust in every shortcut.
- Confidence: low (source documented; shopify absent, dhl absent, cloudflare documented)
- Applies when: Any product with keyboard shortcuts or a search index of pages.
- Exceptions: Shortcuts for actions that are not pages (focus filters, toggle sidebar) are defined in the registry directly.
- Do: Area renamed from "Marketing" to "Growth": the shortcut sheet says "Go to Growth", and searching "marketing" still finds Growth.
- Don't: Shortcut sheet still says "Go to Marketing"; a settings shortcut redirects to a different section; a shortcut points to a page that returns 404 because the feature is not installed.
- Check (static): Verify shortcut and search entries are derived from the nav/route config (no duplicated label strings); write a test that every shortcut target resolves to an existing route and its label equals the current nav label.
- Check (live): Open the "?" sheet and trigger every navigation shortcut; each must land on a page whose H1 matches the label in the sheet, with no redirect and no 404; search an old area name and confirm the renamed area is returned.

### CHR-006 — Users can turn shortcuts off

**Rule:** Offer a personal preference to turn off (or remap) single-character keyboard shortcuts, stored per user in the profile settings.

- Why: Single-key shortcuts fire by accident for speech-input and keyboard-only users and for people typing fast; an off switch is the accessible fallback (WCAG 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts).
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify absent, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any product that uses shortcuts made of letters, digits or punctuation without a modifier key.
- Exceptions: Shortcuts that need a modifier (Cmd/Ctrl+K) or that are active only while a specific widget has focus do not need the switch.
- Do: Profile > Preferences: switch "Keyboard shortcuts" with helper text "Turn off single-key shortcuts such as g h".
- Don't: Letter shortcuts that are always on with no way to disable them.
- Check (static): Verify a user preference flag exists and that the global shortcut handler checks it before handling non-modifier keys.
- Check (live): Turn the preference off, reload, press "?" and "g" then "h" outside a field; nothing happens; Cmd/Ctrl+K still opens search; turn it back on and confirm shortcuts work again.

### CHR-007 — Scope switcher at the top of the sidebar

**Rule:** When a user can belong to more than one account, store or workspace, show the current scope by name in one fixed sidebar position, preferably the sidebar header, as a button that opens a searchable list of scopes with a create option.

- Why: The scope changes what every page shows, so it must be visible before the user reads any data, and a fixed sidebar slot (ideally the header) is where users look for "where am I"; search keeps the list usable at dozens of scopes.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Multi-account, multi-store or multi-workspace products, or any user who has access to more than one scope.
- Exceptions: Single-account products show the account name in the user menu instead of a switcher. A second, nested scope (for example a site inside an account) can be switched from the scoped area's header or by a shortcut, but must still show its current name.
- Do: Sidebar header button "Switch account" showing the current account name; dialog with "Search for an account", a listbox with the current one selected, a count, and "Create account".
- Don't: Current scope visible only inside the profile menu, or a switcher that is a plain unsearchable dropdown of 40 names.
- Check (static): Verify the shared sidebar renders the current scope name in one fixed slot (header preferred) and, when the user has more than one scope, a button with aria-haspopup/aria-expanded that opens a list with a search input, a selected state and a create action.
- Check (live): With a user that has 2+ scopes, confirm the current scope name is visible in the same sidebar position on every page; open the switcher, type part of a name to filter, select another scope, and confirm the sidebar and page content change and the name updates.

### CHR-008 — One user menu for identity, preferences and logout

**Rule:** Group the signed-in identity, personal preferences (theme, language, display) and Log out in a single user menu that is reachable from every page, with Log out as the last item.

- Why: Users look for one place that answers "who am I signed in as" and "how do I leave"; spreading these across the chrome makes logout and account checks slow and error-prone on shared machines.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Every authenticated dashboard.
- Exceptions: Position may be bottom of the sidebar (when there is no top bar) or top right (when there is a top bar); pick one. Account-wide administration (members, billing) belongs in settings, not in this menu, apart from links to those pages.
- Do: Button labelled with the user's name opens a menu: "Signed in as ...", account and plan line, separator, Manage account, Theme, Help center, Log out.
- Don't: Logout inside settings, theme toggle in the footer, and the signed-in email shown nowhere.
- Check (static): Verify a single user-menu component in the shell that contains the identity text, preference items and a Log out item as the last menuitem; verify no second logout control exists elsewhere.
- Check (live): On any page open the user menu by keyboard (Tab to it, Enter); confirm role=menu, the signed-in identity is shown, Log out is the last item, and Escape closes the menu and returns focus to its button.

### CHR-009 — Bell only for a real alert feed; toasts for action feedback

**Rule:** Add a notification bell only when the product has a persistent feed of time-sensitive items the user must act on; report the outcome of the user's own actions with toasts in a single named live region instead.

- Why: A bell implies there is something to check; with no real feed it trains users to ignore it, while action feedback belongs next to the action and disappears on its own.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Deciding whether to put a notifications entry in the chrome.
- Exceptions: Alert rules and delivery settings (what to notify, by email or webhook) are a settings page, not a chrome item. Products with a feed show an unread count on the bell only for unread items.
- Do: Alerts entry with a count for payment disruptions and failed jobs; "Rule saved" appears as a toast in a region named "Notifications".
- Don't: A bell that only ever shows "Rule saved" history, or saves confirmed with a modal.
- Check (static): If the chrome has a bell, verify it is backed by a stored feed (API/model), not by the toast queue; verify the app root renders exactly one toast container with role=region/status and an accessible name.
- Check (live): Perform a save; a toast appears inside one named live region (accessibility tree shows region or status) and disappears or can be dismissed; if a bell exists, open it and confirm it lists items that persist after reload.

### CHR-011 — Persistent help and support entry

**Rule:** Provide one help and support entry in the chrome on every page that leads to documentation and to contacting support (and to service status when one exists), kept separate from the AI assistant.

- Why: Users who are stuck need a path to a human or to the docs from wherever they are; a single entry avoids hunting through pages, and keeping it separate from AI keeps a human route available.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Every dashboard.
- Exceptions: Position varies (sidebar bottom, top bar, or inside the user menu); inside the user menu is acceptable only if the menu is always visible. Links that leave the product open in a new tab and say so.
- Do: Sidebar-bottom button "Support" opening a menu: Knowledge base, Submit a ticket, System status.
- Don't: Support reachable only from a footer link on the home page, or only through the AI chat.
- Check (static): Verify a help/support control in the shared shell; verify its targets include docs and a contact or ticket route; verify external links have target=_blank with rel and an "opens in new tab" cue.
- Check (live): From a detail page and a settings page, find a control named "Help" or "Support" in a landmark (banner, navigation or complementary) or inside the always-visible user menu; open it and confirm it offers docs and a way to contact support.

### CHR-012 — Chrome survives narrow widths with names intact

**Rule:** At narrow widths, move chrome items into icon buttons or a drawer without dropping any of them, and keep each one's accessible name and tooltip.

- Why: Phones and split screens are where users most need search and support quickly; unnamed icons are invisible to screen readers and ambiguous to everyone else.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Any width below about 768 px, and tablets in portrait.
- Exceptions: Keyboard hints (⌘K) and label text may be hidden; the control itself may not.
- Do: At 390 px: "Menu", "Expand search", "Support", "Open assistant" and the user menu are icon buttons, each with an aria-label.
- Don't: Search vanishes from the chrome below 768 px, or the AI and Support buttons render as bare icons without names.
- Check (static): For each chrome control, verify the narrow-width variant keeps an aria-label or visually hidden text; verify no chrome item is display:none at small breakpoints without a drawer/overflow equivalent.
- Check (live): Set the viewport to 390 px; read the accessibility tree of banner and navigation; confirm search, help, user menu, scope switcher and assistant (if any) are each present with a non-empty accessible name, directly or inside the opened menu drawer.

## index

### IDX-001 — One list toolbar above the table

**Rule:** Put search, filters and the view selector together in a single toolbar directly above the table.

- Why: Users scan one predictable strip to narrow a list; scattering search, filters and views around the page makes them hunt for the controls that change what the table shows.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any list or table page with more than one screen of records or more than one way to narrow it.
- Exceptions: A short fixed list (under about 10 rows, no filtering need) can skip the toolbar entirely.
- Do: Toolbar row: view selector, search field, "Filters" button, column picker; table immediately below.
- Don't: Search in the page header, filters in a side panel and the view switcher below the table.
- Check (static): On each index page the search input, filter trigger and view selector share one container that is the previous sibling (or first child of the same section) of the table element.
- Check (live): At 1440 px, open each list page; the search, filter and view controls sit in one horizontal row between the page header and the first table row, with no other content between them and the table.

### IDX-002 — Search placeholder names the searchable fields

**Rule:** Label the list search field with the fields it actually matches, such as "Search by name or code", instead of a bare "Search".

- Why: Users cannot guess whether a list search matches IDs, names, emails or tags; naming the fields prevents empty results that look like missing data.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The list search matches a limited set of fields, or matches by prefix rather than substring.
- Exceptions: A combined search-and-filter field that parses free text and filter tokens may use a generic label if it shows the matched fields as suggestions while typing.
- Do: "Search by email" on a members list; "Search by name prefix" when only prefix matching is supported.
- Don't: A field labelled "Search" that silently matches only the record ID.
- Check (static): Every list search input has a placeholder or accessible name that names at least one field ("by ..."), and the named fields match the fields the backend query uses.
- Check (live): Type a value that appears only in a field not named in the placeholder; the list must return no match, confirming the label is accurate. Type a value from a named field; it must match.

### IDX-003 — Saved views in a selector

**Rule:** Offer a view selector in the list toolbar with preset views, and let users save the current filters, sort and columns as a named view.

- Why: People return to the same slices of a list every day; a named view turns a multi-step filter into one click and keeps the default list uncluttered.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Lists that users filter the same way repeatedly (queues, operational lists, logs).
- Exceptions: Small reference lists with no filters do not need views. Saving user views is confirmed live in only two portals; whether views are personal or shared across the team is not established.
- Do: View menu: All, Unfulfilled, Unpaid, Archived, then user views; "Save" and "Reset view" become enabled only after the user changes a filter, sort or column.
- Don't: A "Save view" button that is always enabled, or views that store only the search text and drop sort and columns.
- Check (static): The list toolbar has a view selector (menu, combobox or button) listing at least the "All" preset; Save/Reset view controls carry disabled state bound to "current view equals saved view".
- Check (live): Change a filter; Save and Reset view enable. Save as a named view, reload, select it from the selector; the same filter, sort and columns return. Press Reset view; the unmodified view returns and the buttons disable again.

### IDX-004 — Lifecycle states as one-click segments with counts

**Rule:** When records move through a fixed lifecycle, expose each state as a one-click segment (tab or preset view) and show the count of records in states that need action.

- Why: In operational lists the main question is "what is waiting for me"; a count per state answers it before the user opens the list.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Records have a small fixed set of workflow states (about 3-7) and users act on them in order (orders, tickets, shipments, approvals).
- Exceptions: For resources with only health or status attributes and no workflow (servers, domains, tokens), a status filter or column is enough. Toolbar actions may change per state, for example a "Manifest all" action only in the Printed state.
- Do: Tabs "New 12 | Printed | Shipped | Returned | Archived"; counts load per tab with a placeholder and never block the table.
- Don't: A single unfiltered list where users must build a status filter by hand every morning.
- Check (static): Each state segment is a link or tab whose URL encodes the state; count badges are rendered from a separate request and have a loading placeholder.
- Check (live): Click each state segment; the URL changes and a reload keeps the same state. Throttle the network; the table renders before or independently of the counters. Check at 768 and 390 px that state segments stay reachable.

### IDX-005 — User-chosen columns with a reset

**Rule:** Show a default subset of columns and let users show or hide the rest from a column picker in the list toolbar or table header.

- Why: Different jobs need different fields; a picker keeps the default table readable while still giving power users every attribute.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The record type has more attributes than fit legibly at desktop width (roughly more than 7-8 columns).
- Exceptions: Tables with a handful of fixed columns need no picker. A locked column and a "Reset to default" item were seen in one portal only; treat them as recommended, not required.
- Do: Column menu with one checkbox per column, the row-identifying column checked and disabled, and "Reset to default" at the bottom.
- Don't: Showing all 20+ attributes by default with horizontal scrolling.
- Check (static): The list toolbar or table header contains a column-picker control whose menu has one checkbox item (menuitemcheckbox or checkbox) per hideable column, and the default column set is defined in one place smaller than the full set.
- Check (live): Open the column picker, uncheck a column; it disappears from the table. Reload; it stays hidden. Check it again; it returns.

### IDX-006 — Sortable headers that show the current sort

**Rule:** Make sortable columns' headers buttons with an accessible name such as "Sort by date", and show the active column and direction.

- Why: Clicking a header is the expected way to reorder a list; without a visible direction indicator users cannot tell how the list is ordered.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Columns with a meaningful order (dates, amounts, names, counts, statuses).
- Exceptions: Columns with no natural order (tags, flags, action buttons, images) stay plain headers.
- Do: "Order date ↓" header button with aria-sort="descending"; clicking flips the direction.
- Don't: Every header clickable, including "Tags" and "Actions", with no indicator of which one is active.
- Check (static): Sortable column headers contain a button; the active one has aria-sort set (ascending/descending) and a visible arrow; non-sortable headers have no button.
- Check (live): Click a sortable header twice; row order flips and the arrow/aria-sort flips with it. Reload; the chosen sort is kept or the URL encodes it.

### IDX-007 — Paginate with range, total and page size

**Rule:** Paginate long lists (default 20-50 rows per page) and show the visible range with the total, Previous/Next controls and a rows-per-page selector.

- Why: A range with a total ("Showing 1-25 of 63") tells users how much is left and confirms a filter worked; page size lets heavy users trade scrolling for fewer clicks.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any list that can exceed one page of records.
- Exceptions: Append-only streams such as live logs may use load-more or infinite scroll if they keep a visible count of loaded records.
- Do: Footer: "Showing 51-100 of 412", Previous, Next, "Rows per page: 50".
- Don't: Rendering thousands of rows at once, or pagination with only page numbers and no total.
- Check (static): The list footer (or toolbar) contains Previous and Next controls with disabled states, a range-and-total text, and a page-size select; the API call carries limit/offset or a cursor.
- Check (live): On a list with more than one page, click Next; the range text updates and Previous enables. Change rows per page; the range and page count recalculate. On the last page Next is disabled.

### IDX-008 — Row selection only where bulk actions exist

**Rule:** Give a list a checkbox column with a header select-all only when it has at least one bulk action.

- Why: Checkboxes promise that something can be done to many rows at once; showing them on lists with no bulk action is noise.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: The list supports at least one action on several records (print, archive, delete, export selected, tag).
- Exceptions: When a bulk action only works for a compatible subset (for example the same carrier or the same status), disable it with a visible reason instead of failing after submit. The behaviour of the bulk-action bar after selection was not exercised in any portal. A select-all label that states its scope ("on page") was seen in one portal only.
- Do: "Select all 50 on page" in the header checkbox; after selecting, offer "Select all 412 matching" as an explicit second step.
- Don't: Checkbox columns on a read-only list, or a header "Select all" that silently selects every record across all pages.
- Check (static): Every list that renders a checkbox column also defines at least one bulk action in its toolbar or selection bar; every list without bulk actions renders no checkbox column.
- Check (live): On each list with checkboxes, tick one row; a bulk-action control appears or enables. Untick all; it hides or disables. Open each list without bulk actions; no row checkboxes are shown.

### IDX-009 — Row actions in a trailing overflow menu

**Rule:** Put per-row actions in the last column as an overflow menu or icon buttons, and keep primary buttons out of table rows.

- Why: A primary button on every row competes with the page's primary action and turns the table into a wall of buttons; a trailing menu keeps rows scannable and predictable.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Lists where each record has secondary actions (edit, duplicate, archive, delete, open externally).
- Exceptions: A work queue whose whole job is one repetitive action per row (for example print a label) may show that single action as a visible row button, provided it is the only button per row and the column can be hidden.
- Do: Last cell: a "..." button opening Edit, Duplicate, Archive, Delete (destructive item last, styled critical).
- Don't: Three filled buttons (Edit, Duplicate, Delete) in every row.
- Check (static): Within table rows there is no element styled as primary; row actions live in the last column inside a menu trigger or icon buttons with accessible names.
- Check (live): Open the row menu with keyboard (Tab to the trigger, Enter); the menu lists the row actions and Escape closes it, returning focus to the trigger.

### IDX-010 — Import and export as list-level actions

**Rule:** Place Import and Export as secondary actions in the header or toolbar of the list whose records they move.

- Why: Users look for import and export where they see the data; hiding them in settings or a separate area makes a routine bulk task a search.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Records users need to move in bulk to or from spreadsheets, accounting or other systems.
- Exceptions: Scheduled or very large exports may also live in a reports area, provided the list links to it. Background export jobs with a status and download column were seen in one portal only, and export scope (filtered vs all) was not exercised anywhere.
- Do: Header: "Export" and "Import" left of the primary "Add"; a large export runs as a job that ends in "Export ready" with a download link.
- Don't: Export hidden only in global settings, with nothing on the list page itself.
- Check (static): Each list whose records can be imported or exported renders the Import and Export controls inside its page header or list toolbar, styled as secondary (not primary).
- Check (live): Open each list that supports import or export; Import and Export are visible without opening a menu outside the page, and clicking Export starts a download, a dialog or a job from that page.

### IDX-011 — No-match state distinct from empty list

**Rule:** When filters or search return nothing, say so and offer to clear them, instead of showing the first-use empty state.

- Why: A first-use message ("Create your first ...") on a filtered list makes users think their data is gone; a no-match message points at the filter as the cause.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Any list with search or filters.
- Exceptions: None for filtered lists. The first-use empty state itself is covered by the states rules.
- Do: "No orders match these filters." with a "Clear filters" button, toolbar still visible with the active filters shown.
- Don't: An illustration saying "Create your first order" while a status filter is active on a list of 400 orders.
- Check (static): The list component renders two different empty templates, selected by whether any filter, search or non-default view is active; the no-match template contains a clear-filters action.
- Check (live): Search for a random string that matches nothing; the message mentions the filter or search and offers to clear it, and the toolbar stays visible. Clear it; the full list returns.

## detail

### DET-001 — Way back to the parent list

**Rule:** Show a back control or breadcrumb to the parent list above or beside the object title on every detail page.

- Why: Detail pages are usually reached from a filtered list or a link deep in another page; a visible way up keeps users oriented and spares them the browser back button, which may lose list state.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any page that shows one record (order, product, service, integration, customer) below a list or hub page.
- Exceptions: A top-level page with no parent (home, a single account overview) needs none. On narrow screens the breadcrumb may collapse to a single back arrow with the parent name.
- Do: Back arrow plus the parent name ("Orders") above the title; or breadcrumb "Settings / Integrations / <name>" with the last crumb not a link.
- Don't: A detail page whose only way out is the sidebar or the browser back button.
- Check (static): The detail template renders a back link or a nav element with aria-label "breadcrumb" before the h1, and its href points to the parent list route.
- Check (live): Open a detail page from its list; find a link or button named after the parent list (or "Back") above the h1 or in the breadcrumb nav; click it and assert the URL is the parent list route.

### DET-002 — Previous and next within the list

**Rule:** When users process records one after another, add previous and next controls on the detail page that follow the order of the list they came from.

- Why: Working through a queue (orders to ship, items to review) is a sequence of detail views; stepping sideways avoids a round trip to the list for every record.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Records that are reviewed or processed in bulk from a list (orders, products, tickets, shipments).
- Exceptions: Long-lived configuration objects that are opened one at a time (a service, a tunnel, a domain) do not need it; one reference has none on such pages. When the detail page carries a completion action (print, approve), an "action and next" or "action and close" variant may sit with it.
- Do: Two icon buttons "Previous order" and "Next order" next to the title, disabled at the ends of the list.
- Don't: Previous and next that ignore the list's filter and sort and jump to an unrelated record.
- Check (static): The detail route receives the list context (filter, sort, position or cursor) and computes previous and next ids from it; both controls have accessible names and a disabled state.
- Check (live): Open the second record of a sorted, filtered list; click Next; assert the URL and title change to the third record of that same list; on the last record assert Next is disabled.

### DET-003 — Title names the object

**Rule:** Use the object's human-readable name or public reference as the page h1, and move internal ids into a details section.

- Why: Users recognise objects by name or by the number they share with customers, not by a generated id; the title is also what the browser tab, breadcrumb and history show.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Every detail page.
- Exceptions: When the name alone is ambiguous in daily work, add one or two short qualifiers (for example reference, customer and destination) in the title; keep the whole title on one line at desktop width.
- Do: h1 "#1042" for an order, "Spring linen shirt" for a product, the service name for a service; the generated UUID appears under "Details" with a copy button.
- Don't: h1 "3f2c9e1a-7b4d-..." or "Edit record".
- Check (static): The detail template binds the h1 to the name or public reference field, never to the primary key; the document title contains the same text.
- Check (live): On three detail pages, read the h1 text and document.title; assert neither is a UUID or a generic label such as "Detail" or "Edit", and that the internal id, if shown, sits outside the h1.

### DET-004 — Status badges beside the title

**Rule:** Show the object's current state as one or more badges directly next to the title, one badge per independent state dimension.

- Why: State decides what the user can do next; putting it at the title means it is read before any action, and separate badges keep combined states (paid but unfulfilled) unambiguous.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Objects with a lifecycle or health state (draft, active, archived; paid, fulfilled; healthy, down).
- Exceptions: Infrastructure objects whose state is a live metric may show it as the first tile of a key-figure strip at the top of the overview instead (see DET-011); one reference does this and puts only the plan badge by the name. Objects with no state need no badge.
- Do: "#1042" followed by badges "Paid" and "Unfulfilled"; a discount title followed by "Active".
- Don't: Status only as a field halfway down the side column, or one merged badge "Paid-Unfulfilled-Partially refunded".
- Check (static): The header component renders a badge list in the same row as the h1; each badge maps to one state field and has a text label (not colour alone).
- Check (live): At 1440 px, getBoundingClientRect() of each status badge has a top within the h1's vertical span and a left within 24 px after the h1's right edge (or wraps directly below it); each badge has visible text.

### DET-005 — Few header actions, the rest in overflow

**Rule:** Put at most one primary and three secondary page-wide actions in the detail header, and move every other page-wide action into a single "More actions" overflow menu there.

- Why: A short, stable action row keeps the main task obvious; an overflow menu in a fixed place lets rare actions (duplicate, archive, delete, print) stay reachable without crowding.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Actions that apply to the whole object (edit, duplicate, share, view live, archive, delete, print).
- Exceptions: A detail page whose only job is to finish a queue item may put the completion action (for example "Print and close") in a sticky footer, as one reference does; keep the overflow in the header even then. Objects whose actions all belong to sections (see DET-006) may have no header actions at all, as on one reference.
- Do: Header right: "Duplicate", "View", "More actions"; the overflow holds Archive and Delete.
- Don't: Seven buttons across the header, or delete as a standalone button next to the primary.
- Check (static): The header renders at most 1 primary and 3 secondary buttons; any further action is an item of a menu button named "More actions" (aria-haspopup="menu") in the header.
- Check (live): On each detail page, count visible buttons in the header region (excluding back and previous/next); assert at most 4, at most one with primary styling; open "More actions" and assert it is a role "menu" with at least one item, and that no delete or archive button sits in the header outside it.

### DET-006 — Section actions stay in their section

**Rule:** Place an action that affects one part of the object (add a line, add a variable, edit an address) inside that part's section heading or toolbar, not in the page header.

- Why: Users find an action where they see the data it changes, and the header stays reserved for actions on the whole object.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Detail pages built from sections or cards that each own a list or a group of fields.
- Exceptions: An action needed from every section (save all) belongs to the page-level save model, not to each section.
- Do: Section "Replicas" with "Add a replica" in its own header; section "Customs details" with an "Edit" button on its right.
- Don't: Header button "Add variable" far from the variables list it changes.
- Check (static): Each section's add and edit controls are rendered inside that section's container; the page header renders no action whose handler changes only one section's data.
- Check (live): For each section that holds a list or editable group, assert its add or edit control is a descendant of that section (same card or region as the section heading).

### DET-007 — Tabs for objects with several independent areas

**Rule:** Split an object detail page into tabs only when it has several independent areas of similar weight (overview, metrics, logs, settings), open on the overview or most used tab, and keep tabs as URL routes.

- Why: A long single page mixing live metrics, logs and configuration is hard to scan, while tabs on a simple record hide content that should be seen together.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Services, integrations and other long-lived objects with their own metrics, logs, deployments or settings.
- Exceptions: Records with one main body plus metadata (order, product, customer, discount) use one scrolling page in two columns instead (see LAY-004); one reference uses no tabs on any record detail.
- Do: Tabs "Overview", "Metrics", "Deployments", "Logs", "Settings", each with its own URL; Overview selected on arrival.
- Don't: Tabs "General" and "Other" on a product with six fields; tab state kept only in memory, so reload returns to the first tab.
- Check (static): Each tab maps to a route or query parameter; the first tab is an overview or the most used view; a tablist has at most 8 tabs.
- Check (live): Open the detail page, click the third tab, reload; assert the same tab is selected and its content shown; assert the tablist has role tablist and arrow keys move between tabs.

### DET-008 — The object's own history on its page

**Rule:** Show a chronological history of the object's events (created, changed, status changes, messages sent, deployments) on the object's detail page, newest first, with the actor and time on each entry.

- Why: Users check what happened to this record and who did it while looking at it; an account-wide log alone forces a filtered search for each record.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Objects that change over time or are touched by several people, integrations or the system.
- Exceptions: Placement varies with the page structure, at the end of the main column, as a collapsible "History" section, or as a dedicated tab (deployments, live logs) on tabbed objects. A comment box for internal notes inside the timeline was seen in one reference only; add it when teams discuss records.
- Do: "Timeline" at the bottom of the main column; heading "October 19"; entries "Payment refunded by <actor>", each with time and a link to the related email or document.
- Don't: History reachable only from a global audit log filtered by record id.
- Check (static): The detail page includes a history component fed by an events query scoped to this object id, sorted descending by time, with actor and timestamp per entry.
- Check (live): Change one field on a record; reload the detail page; assert a new top entry names the change, your user and a time from today.

### DET-009 — Read first, edit in place

**Rule:** Show each field's current value on the detail page and let users edit a field or small section in place (inline field, popover or side panel), without a separate edit page.

- Why: Most visits to a record are to read it or fix one value; in-place editing keeps context and avoids a full form for a single change.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Fields and short groups (name, address, tags, notes, status, one setting) on a record that users mostly read.
- Exceptions: Structural edits that change many related values at once (editing an order's line items) may open a dedicated edit mode from a header "Edit" button. Large forms open in a page, not a modal.
- Do: Value "Delivered at Place" shown as text with an edit affordance; pencil "Edit tunnel name" turns the name into a field with Save and Cancel.
- Don't: All fields shown as empty-looking inputs, or a single "Edit" button that opens a separate page to change one tag.
- Check (static): Each editable field component has a read state (value text) and an edit state, toggled in place; it has an accessible name such as "Edit <field>"; saving follows the page's save model.
- Check (live): On a detail page, activate the edit control of one field; assert the URL does not change and the field becomes editable in place; press Escape and assert the original value is shown unchanged.

### DET-010 — Identifiers with a copy button

**Rule:** Show system identifiers and contact values that users paste elsewhere (ids, tokens, emails, addresses) in a details area, each with a one-click copy button.

- Why: These values are copied into tickets, APIs and other tools; selecting long strings by hand is error-prone.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any detail page with an id, key, email, address or similar value used outside the dashboard.
- Exceptions: Secrets show a copy button only at creation or behind an explicit reveal; never place them in plain text.
- Do: "Tunnel ID 3f2c..." with a button "Copy ID"; customer email with "Copy email".
- Don't: An id rendered in a disabled input that cannot be selected, or no way to copy it at all.
- Check (static): Id and contact fields render a copy button with an accessible name "Copy <field>" that writes the full value with navigator.clipboard.writeText and announces success.
- Check (live): Click each copy button on a detail page; read the clipboard (or intercept writeText) and assert it equals the full displayed value; assert a status or toast message confirms the copy.

### DET-011 — Key figures at the top of the overview

**Rule:** Open a detail overview with a short strip of the object's key figures (three to five), each labelled and with a definition available on demand.

- Why: A few numbers answer "how is this object doing" before the user scrolls into configuration or line items.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Objects that accumulate activity (customers, services, campaigns, connections).
- Exceptions: Transactional records whose meaning is their content (a shipment being prepared, an order) show their content first; one reference has no figures on its record detail.
- Do: Strip "Amount spent | Orders | Customer since | Segment", each label opening its definition; or "Active replicas | Routes | Status | Uptime".
- Don't: Ten unlabeled numbers, or metrics only reachable through a separate analytics page.
- Check (static): The overview renders a figures component with 3-5 items, each with a label, a value and either an info button or a definition popover.
- Check (live): On the overview at 1440 px, assert the figures strip is the first content block under the header, has 3-5 items, and each label's info control opens a definition.

### DET-012 — Danger zone at the end of object settings

**Rule:** Collect the object's destructive or disruptive actions (delete, pause, remove, rotate, clear) in a separate, clearly titled section at the end of its settings or overview, each with a line stating the consequence.

- Why: Placing them last and apart prevents misclicks among routine settings while keeping them easy to find when needed.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify absent, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Objects with their own settings area or tab and at least one irreversible or service-disrupting action.
- Exceptions: Records without a settings area may put delete or archive in the header overflow menu instead (see DET-005). Confirmation follows SAV-006.
- Do: Last settings section "Danger zone" with "Delete service: removes all deployments and routes"; an overview ending in "Advanced actions" with Pause and Remove.
- Don't: A red Delete button between two ordinary settings, or Pause in the middle of a list of metrics.
- Check (static): Destructive actions of an object appear only in a section rendered last in its settings or overview (or in the header overflow), each with consequence text and the critical variant.
- Check (live): Scroll to the end of the object's settings; assert the last section heading names the danger or advanced actions; assert no destructive button appears above it outside the header overflow.
